name: Personalised Wealth Advice
title: Personalised Wealth Advice
answer: Personalised wealth advice covers systems that tailor portfolio recommendations to an individual's goals, time horizon, tax position and tolerance for loss, rather than selling one model portfolio to everyone. It sits inside portfolio construction, where the output is a proposed allocation and the reasoning behind it. The scope runs from simple risk questionnaires that pick a fund mix to ongoing rebalancing and tax-aware trading across many accounts. It also touches retirement planning, cash flow forecasting and the reporting a client sees.

sections.body: Personalised wealth advice covers systems that tailor portfolio recommendations to an individual's goals, time horizon, tax position and tolerance for loss, rather than selling one model portfolio to everyone. It sits inside portfolio construction, where the output is a proposed allocation and the reasoning behind it. The scope runs from simple risk questionnaires that pick a fund mix to ongoing rebalancing and tax-aware trading across many accounts. It also touches retirement planning, cash flow forecasting and the reporting a client sees.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on market and reference data feeds, a client record holding holdings, contributions and withdrawals, and a risk engine that turns answers into constraints. Custodian and broker connections supply positions and execute trades, while tax rules and product data sit alongside. Most deployments are cloud hosted, with a calculation layer for optimisation and simulation and a separate presentation layer for advisers and clients. Data quality and reconciliation matter more than raw compute, because a wrong position or price propagates straight into the advice.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual build starts with a risk assessment, then maps that to an expected return and volatility for each asset class, often through mean variance optimisation or a simulation of many market paths. Constraints are applied for concentration, liquidity, tax lots and account type, and the result is a target allocation that is rebalanced on a schedule or when drift passes a threshold. Advisers review the output, and the system records what was proposed, what was changed and why. Increasingly, language models draft the explanation a client reads, but the numbers still come from the optimiser.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Advice is regulated, so the firm must show the recommendation suited the client, keep records of the basis for it, and manage conflicts such as revenue from in-house products. Client data is sensitive, which brings privacy duties, access controls and retention limits, and model outputs need testing for bias across client groups. Provenance matters: which data, which assumptions and which version of the model produced a given recommendation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward advice that updates continuously rather than annually, with tax and cash flow handled inside the same engine. Expect more direct indexing, where a client holds the underlying securities and the system manages tax losses and screens, and more use of language models for explanation and client service. The open questions are accountability when a model and an adviser disagree, and how firms evidence suitability when the recommendation changes daily. Adoption will depend less on modelling skill than on supervision, data plumbing and the willingness of clients to trust an automated process.
